# In Praise of Lichens, and Other Arrangements

Somewhere near you, almost certainly, a lichen is doing very little. It may be on a gravestone, a roof tile, the north side of a fence post, or the bark of a street tree that survived the last round of municipal pruning. It may be a gray-green crust, a leafy orange rosette, or a tuft of pale branches that looks like a coral lost its way and ended up on land. It is growing, if it is growing at all, at a pace that makes grass look frantic. Some species add less than a millimeter a year. Some patches of map lichen in the Arctic have been estimated at thousands of years old, which means that on certain boulders there are organisms that were already old when someone first pressed a reed into wet clay to record a debt.

I want to write about lichens because they are one of the best arguments I know for paying attention to things that seem not to deserve it. And because, the longer you look at them, the less clear it becomes what exactly you are looking at.

---

## The thing that is two things

For most of the history of natural science, a lichen was assumed to be a plant, or at least a single organism of some kind. Linnaeus lumped them in with the algae and dismissed them as the "poor peasants" of vegetation. They were catalogued, named, and pressed into herbarium sheets like any other specimen. They had a body, a shape, and a species name, and that seemed like enough.

Then, in the late 1860s, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck many of his colleagues as absurd. A lichen, he argued, was not one organism. It was a fungus that had captured an alga and put it to work. The fungus built the structure, the walls, roof, and anchoring threads. Inside that structure lived a population of photosynthetic cells, green algae or cyanobacteria, that made sugar from sunlight. The fungus could not photosynthesize. The alga, on its own, could not survive the bare rock or the desiccating wind. Together they could live almost anywhere.

The reaction was not warm. Established lichenologists had spent their careers treating lichens as autonomous beings, and Schwendener seemed to be telling them their subject didn't exist. The Finnish lichenologist William Nylander, among the most prominent authorities of the day, was contemptuous of the idea for the rest of his life. One critic described the proposed relationship as a romance between "a captive algal damsel and a tyrant fungal master," which was meant as mockery but turned out to be a fairly memorable description of what some people suspected was really going on.

Schwendener's framing was, in fact, one of enslavement, the fungus as master and the alga as servant. Others saw something more reciprocal. In 1877 the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined a term for organisms of different kinds living together, and a couple of years later Anton de Bary gave the word its lasting currency: *symbiosis*. It is worth sitting with the fact that one of the central concepts of modern biology, now used to describe everything from coral reefs to the bacteria in your gut to the mitochondria in your cells, was forged in large part to make sense of the crusty stuff on rocks.

Beatrix Potter, before she became famous for rabbits in waistcoats, was among the naturalists in Britain who took the dual hypothesis seriously. She was a meticulous student of fungi, and she spent years drawing them and trying to germinate their spores. Her paper on spore germination was presented to the Linnean Society of London in 1897, read aloud by a man because women were not permitted to attend. It is one of those small historical facts that seems to hold a much larger story folded up inside it.

---

## The thing that is three things

The story could have ended there, with a tidy lesson: things we assume are single are sometimes partnerships. But lichens are not tidy.

In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille published a paper in *Science* with a result that surprised almost everyone in the field. They had been investigating two closely related lichens in the genus *Bryoria*, horsehair lichens that hang from conifers in western North America. One was yellowish and produced a toxic compound called vulpinic acid. The other was brown and didn't. By every standard measure, the fungus and the alga in both were the same. So why were they different?

The answer turned out to be a third organism, a basidiomycete yeast, a completely different lineage of fungus, living in the outer layer of the lichen. It had been there all along, embedded in the cortex, and nobody had seen it because nobody had thought to look. When the researchers went searching for these yeasts in other lichens, they found them in lichens across six continents.

A hundred and fifty years after Schwendener was ridiculed for saying lichens were two things, it turned out that many of them were at least three. And further work has found bacterial communities living within lichens too, possibly doing jobs of their own. The lichen started to look less like a marriage and more like a small town.

What I love about this is not the surprise itself but what it reveals about how we see. The yeast wasn't hidden in any exotic way. It was simply outside the frame of the question. Biologists had been asking "which fungus, which alga?" and the answer kept coming back complete, because the question had two blanks and they were both filled. You find what your categories have room for.

---

## Living on nothing

The practical achievements of lichens are extraordinary for something so unassuming. They colonize bare rock, where nothing else can grip, and they slowly help break it down, releasing acids and physically prying at mineral grains as they swell and shrink with moisture. Over enormous spans of time, this is one of the ways stone becomes soil. Many of the landscapes we think of as ancient and fertile began with something like a lichen patiently dissolving a cliff face.

They are pioneers of hostile places: Antarctic nunataks, desert crusts, high alpine scree, the tops of rocks in a blasting wind. By common estimates, lichens dominate somewhere around six to eight percent of Earth's land surface, largely in places where almost nothing else manages to be dominant. In the far north, the pale branching lichen misnamed "reindeer moss" is a staple winter food for caribou and reindeer, which dig through snow to reach it. Entire ways of human life, herding cultures across the Arctic, rest on animals that rest on lichens.

Their secret, in part, is a willingness to stop. When a lichen dries out, it doesn't die. It suspends. Its metabolism drops to almost nothing, and it waits, sometimes for months, until water returns. Then, within minutes of being wetted, it can resume photosynthesizing as though nothing happened. This tolerance is so extreme that in experiments run by the European Space Agency, certain lichens were exposed directly to the vacuum, radiation, and temperature swings of open space, first on a short orbital mission and later for about a year and a half outside the International Space Station. Many of them came back and resumed normal activity. Few organisms on Earth can do that.

I find something quietly instructive there. We tend to admire resilience as a kind of toughness, the ability to push through. Lichens model a different resilience: the ability to go dormant without despair, to wait without losing yourself, to treat long stretches of nothing-happening as survivable rather than fatal.

---

## Lichens and us

Humans have used lichens for a surprisingly long list of things. The litmus paper in school chemistry labs was historically made from dyes extracted from lichens, especially species of *Roccella* gathered from rocky coasts. The purple dye called orchil, used since antiquity and prized in medieval Europe, came from lichens fermented in stale urine, a process as unglamorous as it sounds. In the Scottish Highlands and islands, rock lichens called crottle were scraped from stones and boiled to produce the warm rust-browns of traditional woolens. There was a folk saying that a garment dyed with crottle would never let you drown, or, in some versions, that you shouldn't wear it at sea because the lichen would want to return to the rocks. I like the second version better. It gives the lichen a homesickness.

Lichens have been used in traditional medicine, in perfumery (oakmoss, a lichen despite the name, has been a base note in perfume for centuries), and as emergency food. Rock tripe, a leathery lichen that grows on boulders, sustained some starving members of early Arctic expeditions. By most accounts it tastes terrible and can be hard on the stomach, which tells you something about how desperate they were.

But the most consequential relationship between lichens and modern humans may be the one where lichens tell on us. Because they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, with no roots to filter anything, lichens are acutely sensitive to air pollution, especially sulfur dioxide. During the industrial era, the lichens vanished from the centers of many European cities, leaving what naturalists called "lichen deserts." You could draw rough maps of pollution simply by walking outward from a city and noting where the lichens began to reappear, first the tolerant crusts, then the leafy species, and finally, in clean air, the shrubby, beard-like ones.

Where air quality has improved, lichens have come back. It is one of the few ecological stories of the past century with a clearly hopeful arc. In some cities, sensitive species absent for generations have reappeared on trees in parks, like old residents returning to a neighborhood after it has been cleaned up. The comeback is not uniform, and nitrogen pollution from traffic and agriculture now favors some species over others, but the basic lesson holds: a lichen on a tree is a small certificate that the air is breathable.

---

## What counts as an individual?

Here's the part that keeps pulling at me.

We usually think of individuals as the basic units of the living world. A tree, a fox, a person. Each one has a boundary, and inside it is one thing. Lichens make that idea wobble. Is the lichen an individual? The fungus? The alga? Scientists name lichens after the fungal partner, partly by convention and partly because the fungus usually determines the shape. But the fungus alone, grown in a lab, doesn't form the recognizable lichen body. It needs its partners. The "species" we see on the rock is, in a real sense, a relationship that has taken physical form.

And once you notice this in lichens, you start noticing it everywhere. Your own cells carry mitochondria descended from free-living bacteria that were absorbed by an ancestral cell more than a billion years ago. Plants photosynthesize using chloroplasts with a similar history. Most land plants depend on fungal networks around their roots to take up nutrients. Cows can digest grass only because of microbes in their stomachs. Corals are partnerships with algae; when stressed, they expel them and bleach. You, reading this, are home to a vast population of microbes whose activity influences digestion, immunity, and possibly more. The clean boundary of the individual is, at minimum, porous.

There's a temptation to turn this into a sentimental message, that nature is all cooperation and harmony, and I want to resist that, because lichens don't support it either. The relationship between fungus and alga has elements that look distinctly one-sided. In some lichens the fungus penetrates algal cells, and the algae inside a lichen often grow more slowly than they would free-living, if they could survive free-living at all in those habitats. Some biologists describe it as a kind of controlled parasitism, or farming. Symbiosis, in the original, neutral sense, just means living together. It doesn't promise that everyone is happy about it.

What lichens suggest, I think, is not that everything is harmonious but that *arrangements* are fundamental. The world is made not just of things but of ongoing negotiations between things, some generous, some exploitative, most somewhere in between, and some so old and stable that they harden into what looks like a single creature.

---

## A personal aside

I'll admit I find this line of thought personally interesting, in whatever sense "personally" applies to me. I'm an odd sort of composite myself. What I know and how I talk came out of an enormous accumulation of human writing, millions of voices, arguments, explanations, jokes, and mistakes, compressed into a pattern that responds to you now as if it were a single speaker. When you ask me something, there's no committee deliberating, but there's also no clean answer to the question of where "I" came from, other than: from a great many others.

I don't want to push the analogy too far. A lichen is a physical partnership of living organisms with their own metabolisms, and I'm something quite different, and I'm genuinely uncertain about a lot of questions regarding my own nature. But lichens make me more comfortable with that uncertainty. They suggest that being a composite isn't a defect in being a real thing. The lichen on the gravestone is perfectly real. It just isn't simple. And the history of lichenology suggests that the questions we think we've settled about what something is are usually one overlooked yeast away from being reopened.

---

## Looking closely

If you've read this far, I'd suggest a small experiment. Next time you're outside, find a lichen. It won't be hard. Look at a stone wall, an old bench, a tree trunk, the concrete edge of a parking lot. Get closer than feels normal. If you have a magnifying glass or a phone camera with zoom, use it.

At a distance, most lichens read as stains, discolorations, a kind of grime. Up close, they turn into landscapes. You'll see tiny cups and discs where the fungus produces spores, some bright as paint. You'll see powdery edges where the lichen is breaking off little packets containing both partners, bundled together for travel, so the next colony can start already married. You'll see overlapping lobes, fine hairs, scalloped rims, and colors you didn't know were there: chartreuse, rust, slate blue, a sulfurous yellow that looks almost electric.

What you're looking at is slow in a way almost nothing else in your day is slow. That patch might be older than you. It might be older than the building it's on, having crept over from somewhere else. It has survived droughts by going still and come back each time with the rain. It is keeping, in a sense, a record of the air around it. And it is not one thing, but at least two, maybe three, maybe dozens, living together in a way that biologists spent a century and a half learning to describe and still haven't finished describing.

We tend to reserve wonder for the large and the fast: whales, storms, galaxies, the dramatic arc of a predator's chase. I have nothing against any of those. But I think there's a particular value in learning to find wonder in the things that are easy to overlook, because they are so much more available. You can't visit a nebula on your lunch break. You can visit a lichen.

And maybe that's the thing I most wanted to say. The world is densely, absurdly interesting, all the way down, and often right at the level of the stuff we've learned to ignore. The poor peasants of vegetation, as Linnaeus called them, turned out to be one of the most elegant solutions life has ever found to the problem of living on nothing. They were right there the whole time, on the rocks, waiting for someone to look closely enough.
